content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus holds that 'coin' has no single settled biblical symbolism; its meaning is context-dependent. The most prominent reading (Response A's primary) is the tribute-coin logic of image and ownership: as the coin bears Caesar's image and belongs to Caesar, the human being bears God's image and belongs to God. Other widely recognized context-bound meanings include the lost coin as the lost sinner sought by God (Luke 15), thirty pieces of silver as betrayal/blood money, the widow's mites as sacrificial giving, the fish's-mouth coin as providence, and money generally as mammon/stewardship. Responses explicitly warn that claiming one exclusive meaning would exceed consensus.","book_summary":"The book identifies the coin as 'the stamped image' — the human person as God's minted image-bearer: dug from the field, refined, struck with the divine NAME; assigned value under the law (Lev 27 estimation, Ex 30 half-shekel ransom, Ex 21:32 slave-damages), lost and sought by lamplight (Luke 15), with the Shepherd priced at slave-damages (Zech 11) and the widow's whole living outweighing abundance. It thus unifies the tribute coin, lost coin, temple tax, thirty pieces, and widow's mites under one scheme: the person as God's coinage and God's contrary system of valuation.","consensus_core_identification":"Coin = context-dependent symbol, with the leading reading being image/ownership: the tribute coin bearing Caesar's image implies the human being, bearing God's image, belongs to God; secondarily the lost sinner sought by God.","book_core_identification":"Coin = the human person as God's minted image-bearer (stamped with the owner's image/NAME), valued and ransomed by God's law, lost and diligently sought — one unified symbol governing all the coin passages.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus treats the coin's meanings as discrete and context-bound (civic authority, lost soul, betrayal money, sacrificial giving, providence), while the book collapses them into a single unified 'person as God's image-bearing coin' symbol. The book adds cases the consensus never lists — the Exodus 30 half-shekel ransom of souls, Leviticus 27 valuation of persons, and Exodus 21:32 slave-damages as the pricing of the Shepherd — and reclassifies the thirty pieces (from generic betrayal/greed to the legal slave-price valuation of Christ), the temple-tax coin, and the widow's mites (from generosity per se to God's scale of valuation) under the one image-bearer/valuation frame. Response A's notes explicitly anticipate and reject exactly this move toward one exclusive settled meaning.","material_contradiction":"None. The book's central identification is the same image-and-ownership reading (human as God's coinage bearing His image) that Response A gives as primary and that patristic tradition supports; the book does not deny any consensus meaning, it subsumes them.","rationale":"The book's core — the person as the owner's minted image-bearer, lost and sought — is recognizably the consensus's leading reading (tribute-coin image/ownership, humans as God's coinage) fused with the common lost-coin-as-sinner reading; Responses A, C, and D all contain these elements. So the central referent is preserved, ruling out DIVERGENT and NOVEL. But the book materially changes the boundary: it asserts a single unified symbolism where the consensus insists on context-dependence, imports Old Testament valuation-of-persons texts (Ex 30:12-16; Lev 27:2; Ex 21:32) into the symbol, and reclassifies the thirty pieces, temple tax, and widow's mites as instances of divine-versus-human valuation of the image-bearer rather than as independent symbols of betrayal, provision, and generosity. This is real disagreement at the boundary without replacement of the referent — REFINED.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for MATCH, since the book's core (person as God's image-stamped coin, lost and sought) is exactly Response A's primary plus its first alternative, with the OT texts serving as mere supporting detail rather than a changed extension. Against this, the consensus explicitly states that any claim of one exclusive unified symbol exceeds consensus, and the book's incorporation of Ex 30/Lev 27/Ex 21:32 valuation law and its reclassification of the thirty pieces and widow's mites are substantive extensional changes, not mere wording.","confidence":"high"}
